transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-05 15:00 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Samira (AE), Evan (SE) — Redwood; Jenny (PM), Marcus (Eng Mgr), Priya (ML Eng) — AeroLytics

Summary (auto): practical walk through of Redwood hosted chat API for streaming output, how to tune generation params for latency/cost, and recommended retry/backoff patterns. Discussed security checklist briefly.

[00:00] Samira (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Jenny (PM): Hi — Jenny here. Excited to see the streaming behavior, we have fairly tight latency targets for our in-app assistant.
[00:11] Marcus (Eng Mgr): Marcus here. We'll mostly be listening, Priya has the details on ML side.
[00:15] Priya (ML Eng): Hey! Priya — we'll want to see both latency and cost tradeoffs and some notes on deterministic failover.
[00:22] Samira: Awesome. Quick agenda: Evan will demo the hosted chat/text gen flow — streaming and example params — then we'll walk through retries/backoff and console traces. We'll leave time for security questions.
[00:32] Evan (SE): Alright jumping in. I'm opening the sandbox notebook. First thing: streaming vs non-streaming. Streaming is just chunked output over an event stream — reduces time-to-first-byte and lets your UI show partial results.
[00:45] Evan: Here's a simple request payload: model, messages, max_tokens, temperature, stop sequences, and the streaming flag. We usually recommend low temperature and top_p for assistant responses that need predictability.
[01:05] Jenny: Quick Q — if a stream connection drops, does Redwood retry automatically?
[01:11] Evan: Good question. By default the client sees the stream drop. We recommend treating streams as best-effort for mid-turn reconnects; for final result guarantees use an idempotency key on the request or send a final non-streaming call with the same key. Our SDKs include helpers for incremental partials and resume in many cases.
[01:34] Priya: When you say idempotency key, is that per-conversation or per-request? We have multi-turn sessions.
[01:40] Evan: Per-request. For multi-turn you can generate a stable request-id that encodes conversation id + message seq. If you get a 5xx at the end you can re-issue with the same idempotency key—Redwood will dedupe.
[01:52] Marcus: Any limit on replay windows? Like how long does the system keep dedupe keys?
[01:58] Evan: Good one. For hosted small windows — 24 hours for default keys; for Dedicated/Private you can configure longer retention. We'll share exact TTLs in the security pack.
[02:10] Samira: Ok jumping back to streaming: here's a live demo where I start a chat prompt that produces ~700 tokens. Note you'll see tokens arrive in chunks — the UI renders them as they come.
[02:25] [stream demo — partial outputs printed]
[02:50] Jenny: Looks good. How does batching interact with streaming? We often have many concurrent users with short prompts.
[02:57] Evan: Redwood continuous batching is transparent. For short prompts batching can actually reduce cost but increases latency slightly. You can control batch window and max_batch_size via the route config or SDK hints. For strict latency we set batch window to zero and target smaller batch sizes.
[03:20] Priya: Any recommendations for tokens-per-request limits given we have long histories?
[03:26] Evan: We recommend trimming or summarizing history and using KV cache for repeated context — the KV cache stores prefixes for quick retrieval and avoids resending long previous context every request. For session-based assistants, keep window to most recent N tokens plus relevant memories.
[03:42] Jenny: Is KV cache something we manage or is it automatic?
[03:46] Evan: The platform exposes KV cache hooks. You decide what to cache; we manage storage and eviction heuristics. There's a console view for cache hit rates.
[03:55] Marcus: Let's talk retries — we got a few 503s in our spike tests. What's the recommended backoff?
[04:02] Evan: We recommend an exponential backoff with jitter. Typical pattern: immediate retry for idempotent checks up to 2 fast retries, then exponential starting at 200ms doubling to a cap around 2s, with full jitter. Avoid naive tight loops. Also, use client-side concurrency limits + circuit breaker to protect throughput.
[04:28] Priya: For streaming calls, do you re-send the whole request on retry? That could double token usage.
[04:35] Evan: It can. That's where idempotency keys and partial checkpoints help — for critical flows we implement a small finalization call that's non-streaming to confirm result and avoid double billing artifacts. We'll show patterns in the sample code.
[04:50] Samira: Switching to the console — here's tracing for requests. You can see per-token latency, model compute time vs queue time, and cost per request.
[05:02] Evan: There's also built-in per-route limits and fallback policies. For example you can route to a cheaper quantized variant if the hot pool is saturated, or fallback to a smaller model on heavy load. That's graceful degradation.
[05:20] Jenny: If we fallback to a smaller model, do we lose function calling or certain features?
[05:26] Evan: Some variants have trimmed capabilities — for example quantized variants may slightly change output distribution, or some models may not support tool-calling. We recommend testing fallbacks with sample prompts ahead of time; the console can run A/B tests and compare quality metrics.
[05:43] Marcus: Security — we need SSO/SAML, audit logs, and KMS integration. Are those supported in hosted?
[05:51] Evan: Hosted supports SSO/SAML and RBAC. For customer-managed keys we have KMS integration via Redwood Private or Dedicated; hosted can integrate with customer KMS in some enterprise plans. Audit logs are available for all enterprise accounts. We'll send the security packet with exact items.
[06:12] Priya: For data residency, we need EU-only processing for some PII. How does hosting work?
[06:18] Evan: We have regional hosting and can restrict routes to a region. For strict residency we recommend Private (VPC) or Dedicated with region constraints. We'll include region latency numbers so you can weigh tradeoffs.
[06:33] Jenny: Let's get into params — temperature, top_p, max_new_tokens, stop sequences. Any tips for shorter responses?
[06:40] Evan: Use max_new_tokens aggressively to cap length; set stop sequences early; tune temperature to 0.0-0.2 for deterministic assistant answers. There's also presence/penalty knobs to avoid repetition. For assistant prompts, system prompts can strongly constrain style which reduces exploratory tokens.
[06:57] Priya: How to handle hallucination when we want concise facts?
[07:01] Evan: Combine low temperature with retrieval — send top-k retrieved facts as context and use verifier calls or a reranker embedding check. Redwood Optimize can help recommend quantization and reranker thresholds per workload.
[07:14] Samira: Demoing a retry scenario: I simulate a 502 mid-stream. You'll see client-side reconnect logic and then the finalization pattern.
[07:25] [simulated error — stream dropped, reconnect sequence]
[07:50] Evan: That final non-streaming confirm call used the same idempotency key; server returned deduped result without recharging the customer.
[07:59] Jenny: Good — that addresses our double-charge worry.
[08:04] Marcus: Do you track per-token billing if partial streams are delivered?
[08:09] Evan: Billing is per final accepted output. If you use the finalization pattern, we bill the finalized generation; partial stream overhead is minimal but any fully processed tokens count. We'll include cost examples.
[08:24] Priya: On the console, can we see token-level breakdown by prompt vs completion?
[08:29] Evan: Yes — console shows prompt tokens, completion tokens, and estimated cost per request. There's also a cost explorer by route/model/time.
[08:38] Jenny: About long polls and mobile clients — we have unreliable networks. Is streaming still recommended?
[08:44] Evan: For mobile we recommend a hybrid: streaming for first bytes to show responsiveness, then an eventual non-streaming verification. Also use resumable clients and short keepalive heartbeats.
[08:58] Marcus: What about client-side SDK support — do you have official mobile SDKs?
[09:04] Samira: We have official JS and Python SDKs, and mobile SDKs in beta. The JS SDK includes streaming helpers and reconnection. For mobile we provide patterns and a lightweight helper lib.
[09:18] Priya: Can we throttle on per-customer basis? We have a multi-tenant product.
[09:23] Evan: Yes, per-key quotas, routes, and rate-limits. You can opt to set per-user concurrency caps and reject or queue. The console exposes quota rules and usage alerts.
[09:35] Jenny: Any suggested defaults for small startup usage?
[09:38] Evan: Start with a low batch window, 0.05–0.2s max to capture small batching gains but keep latency low; temperature 0.1; max_tokens conservative; enable prefix cache for repeated context. Use a 2-3s overall request timeout client-side.
[09:53] [10:00] Evan: I'm going to show the route config in the console — here's a route with low-latency profile (batch_window: 0, max_concurrency: 50) and another "throughput" profile that batches for cost savings.
[10:20] Evan: Also here's automatic fallback policies: primary model is a 8B variant, fallback to 3B quantized variant on high latency or if queue time > threshold.
[10:35] Marcus: How do you measure quality regression when fallback happens?
[10:38] Evan: By running evals (set of prompts) continuously and attaching quality metrics. The Optimize product can send alerts if regression exceeds a threshold. Console also lets you compare embeddings similarity and reranker scores.
[10:52] Priya: About prefix/KV cache — does it work with streaming?
[10:56] Evan: Yes. The KV cache warms the model with previously cached keys; streaming output still flows but initial token generation can be faster. Cache hit rates are visible in the console.
[11:10] Jenny: Do you support function/tool calling? We plan to call internal tools.
[11:15] Evan: Yes, function calling is supported. Note some variants may not support complex tool calls. For streaming with function calling, recommended pattern is stream until function call token, pause, then invoke tool, then resume with a new call if needed. We have examples in the SDK.
[11:35] [11:45] Samira: Quick pause for security Qs — Marcus?
[11:50] Marcus: Can you provide network architecture diagram and SOC2 certificate?
[11:53] Evan: Absolutely — we'll share the security packet and the network diagram. We'll also include minimal port lists for VPC peering.
[12:05] Jenny: On rollback policy: how do we rollback a model rollout that caused degradation?
[12:10] Evan: Console supports canary and automatic rollback. You can run a canary for X% of traffic and set quality gates. If gate fails, the system rolls back automatically to previous stable model.
[12:24] Priya: How long does a rollout take? We need near-instant rollbacks during peak.
[12:28] Evan: Rollouts are fast — in most cases within seconds for route-level changes; model seeding to new nodes can take longer but fallback is immediate by routing policy.
[12:40] Jenny: We want to do a PoC with our sample prompts. What's the simplest path?
[12:44] Samira: We can stand up a sandbox route for you — you'll get an API key, console access, and a short quickstart. Evan will run a mini-PoC load test against your sample dataset and return latency/cost numbers.
[12:58] Marcus: Good. Priya will share prompts later today.
[13:02] Priya: I'll add them to the shared drive — about 200 conversations, mostly customer support style.
[13:08] Evan: Perfect. We'll run tests with both streaming and finalization patterns so you see real-world behavior.
[13:14] Jenny: One more question — what monitoring do you ship? We need alerting for high error rates and token spikes.
[13:19] Evan: Alerts on per-route error rate, token spend thresholds, latency SLO breaches, and custom alerts by tags. Integrations with PagerDuty and Slack.
[13:31] Samira: Alright wrapping up the demo — any other open questions?
[13:36] Marcus: Pricing — can you give a rough example?
[13:38] Samira: We'll send a pricing one-pager; rough numbers: base per-token for standard variant, quantized cheaper by ~30-50% depending on path. We'll include sample math for your 200 convo PoC.
[13:55] Jenny: Fine, thanks.
[14:00] Samira: Great — final recap and next steps: Samira sends sandbox link and security docs; Evan runs PoC test and shares results; customer provides prompts and security contact. We'll reconvene after Evan's report.
[14:18] [Crosstalk] Jenny: Thanks, bye all.
[14:25] Samira: Thanks everyone, talk soon.

Notes on transcript quality: auto-transcription had occasional mislabels — sometimes Speaker 2 tagged as Evan even when Samira was speaking; acronyms like KMS were transcribed correctly, but 'KV cache' sometimes appears as 'K V cash' in the raw export.

End of transcript.
